title: APC Injury: A Hypothesis That Dendritic-Cell Impairment Allows Persistent Viral Antigen and Loss of Self-Tolerance After Infection
content: After an acute infection, the immune system can fail in two directions at once. It may fail to clear viral material that does not belong, allowing antigen or RNA to persist in tissue, and it may fail to tolerate self, producing autoantibodies. Failure to clear antigen is not the same as immunological tolerance of it. This article proposes that injury to antigen-presenting cells, chiefly dendritic cells (APC Injury), can help explain both failures after SARS-CoV-2. Acute COVID-19 commonly depletes circulating conventional and plasmacytoid dendritic cells. Remaining cells can be poor at co-stimulation or at producing interferon when challenged. After the acute illness, findings diverge: some long COVID cohorts show fewer cDC1s or more activated pDCs, others no major blood dendritic-cell depletion. Tissue studies show that altered dendritic-cell frequencies and retained viral antigen can coexist, but not that one causes the other. Autoantibodies appear in some assays and not in others. No published study has measured dendritic-cell function, tissue antigen, and self-antigen-specific regulatory T-cell or autoantibody outcomes in the same patients. Ebola virus can persist for months to years in privileged sites, and Ebola proteins can block dendritic-cell maturation in vitro. That analogy supports a testable model, not a proof in long COVID. A longitudinal study should measure dendritic-cell function, tissue viral material, and incident or changing autoreactivity in the same participants, with recovered controls, treating self-antigen-specific regulatory T-cell function as the mechanistic intermediate rather than as a substitute outcome. The model's central testable implication is temporal: a defined dendritic-cell functional defect should precede and predict both persistent antigen and new autoreactivity in the same people, rather than following either. A reduced residual association between the two outcomes after the defect and relevant common causes are accounted for would be consistent with the model, but would not uniquely identify it, because separate pathways with shared upstream causes can also produce correlated outcomes. No therapeutic claim follows until the affected subset, the impaired function, the tissue compartment, and the direction of correction have been identified.
